t: Maximum Number of Ones — Periodicity + Greedy Selection
o: We must fill a `width x height` 0/1 matrix so that every `sideLength x sideLength` square contains at most `maxOnes` ones, maximizing total ones. The key structural fact: the constraint only involves squares of a fixed size, so the optimal matrix is **periodic** with period `sideLength` in both dimensions — every cell `(i, j)` can be set to 1 iff its residue class `(i % s, j % s)` was chosen, where `s = sideLength`. Choosing a residue class contributes ones at all matrix positions congruent to it; each of the `s*s` residue classes has an easily computable multiplicity. In Example 1 (`3x3`, `s=2`, `maxOnes=1`) the four corners share residue `(0,0)`, giving 4 ones from one class. In Example 2 (`maxOnes=2`) we also pick `(0,1)` or `(1,0)`, whose three cells give 6 total. Constraints are tiny (`width, height <= 100`), so even enumerating every cell is fine; the real task is recognizing the periodicity argument.
k: Any valid pattern can be made periodic with period `sideLength`: replicate the top-left `s x s` block across the whole matrix, which never violates any square constraint.
Each residue class `(r, c)` appears `cntRows(r) * cntCols(c)` times, where `cntRows(r)` counts indices `< width` congruent to `r` mod `s`.
The answer is simply the sum of the `maxOnes` largest multiplicities — a greedy selection.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Cells by Residue Class
a.i: Visit every cell `(i, j)`, map it to its residue class `(i % s, j % s)`, and accumulate how many matrix cells fall into each class. Because the pattern can be taken periodic, filling exactly the chosen classes keeps every `s x s` square within budget, and taking the `maxOnes` most frequent classes maximizes the total. This is the most direct translation of the insight into code.
s: Let s = sideLength; create a 2D array freq[s][s] initialized to zero.
For each i in [0, height) and j in [0, width), increment freq[i % s][j % s].
Collect all s*s frequencies into a list and sort it in descending order.
Sum the first maxOnes values and return the sum.
a.t: O(s^2 log(s^2)) after O(1)-time formula counting per class (or O(width*height + s^2 log s^2) if you literally enumerate cells); sorting dominates.
a.sp: O(s^2) to store the class frequencies.

a.i: Instead of touching every matrix cell, note that the number of rows `i < height` with `i % s == r` is `ceil((height - r) / s)` when `r < min(s, height)` (and 0 otherwise), and similarly for columns. Multiply to get each class's multiplicity in closed form, then greedily sum the `maxOnes` largest using a max-heap or sort. This avoids any dependence on `width * height` beyond the formula and makes the greedy structure explicit.
s: For each residue pair (r, c) with 0 <= r, c < s, compute rowCount = number of i in [0, height) with i % s == r via ceil division (0 if r >= height).
Push rowCount * colCount into a max-heap (or array to sort).
Pop the maxOnes largest values and return their sum.
a.t: O(s^2 log(s^2)) — building s^2 multiplicities and sorting/heap-popping them dominates; independent of width*height.

w: In an interview, lead with the periodicity argument: since all constrained squares have the same size, tiling the matrix with copies of one `s x s` block is WLOG optimal, reducing the problem to picking the best `maxOnes` positions inside that block weighted by how often each position recurs. Then present Approach 2 as the clean solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that some residues may not occur at all when `width` or `height` is not a multiple of `s` (guard with `min(s, dim)` or let ceil-division handle it); off-by-one errors in the ceil-division count `(dim - r + s - 1) / s`; and assuming `maxOnes` classes always exist (it's guaranteed `maxOnes <= s*s`). Edge cases: `maxOnes = 0` returns 0; `s = 1` means the whole matrix is one class, so the answer is `width * height`. Likely follow-ups: prove the periodicity claim rigorously (exchange argument on any optimal matrix), handle multiple distinct square sizes simultaneously, or scale to huge `width`/`height` where only the formula approach survives.
